hero.title: Periscopic Relay Imaging
hero.description: A piezo-actuated XYZ objective-scanning module with 13.5 mm of travel on each axis. PRISM V5 integrates at the objective end of an optical system and is currently used in a confocal setup at IQC's NPQO Lab for diamond nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center measurements.

currentWork.title: From Idea to Instrument
paragraphs: PRISM V5 is used by the Nano Photonics and Quantum Optics Lab at the Institute for Quantum Computing, University of Waterloo, for diamond NV-center qubit measurements through a cryostat window.

I designed and built PRISM from the ground up, including its optomechanical assemblies, initial manual machining, and optical integration. I transitioned the early prototypes to professionally machined components by developing production-ready engineering drawings and incorporating design for manufacturability (DFM) principles. I also developed the initial LabVIEW scanning controls and completed instrument setup and validation, establishing the foundation for subsequent software development and diamond experiments conducted by the lab.

configuration.title: What is PRISM?
description: PRISM works at the objective end of an optical system, where a stationary microscope objective would normally be mounted. Instead of moving the sample or steering the beam through the objective, PRISM moves the objective itself in X, Y, and Z.
Its periscopic optical design allows the beam to remain centered on the objective as it moves, maintaining alignment with the rest of the optical system.

This means researchers can continue using their existing optical setup, including cameras, photodetectors, spectrometers, and other equipment, while adding precise three-dimensional scanning at the objective.

work.text: A periscopic optical path that keeps the beam centered on the moving objective, with cameras and detectors arranged to suit the experiment.

work.title: Instrument control
work.text: Initial LabVIEW raster-scan control with piezo positioning and detector readout, plus initial testing and setup for scanning.

homeLab.title: Bringing the lab home
paragraphs: My home lab is the beginning of my independent precision tooling. Current projects include an encoder-equipped stage and a tool for inspecting that stage's precision. The goal is to build on the skills learned over the years in optics, mechanics, and electronics to create a small-scale precision tooling lab, with one main encompassing project in mind.
These are self-directed builds I work on as time permits. I will share the experiments and development process on KicoLabCO.
